Coral

Execution rails for agents.

Coral gives your agents execution rails for work with sensitive enterprise systems. It's self-hosted, open source, and you can use it with any agent and any system with an API.

More precise permissions control. As your agents do work across more systems, mapping identities to MCP tools is no longer sufficient to control risk. Permissions are all or nothing per tool so if an agent can call update_record, it can update any record in any way the tool allows. With Coral it's easy to define with code what specific actions an agent can take.

Less duplicated agent work. Agents start every task from scratch. They re-read tool schemas, retry failed calls, and spend tokens rewriting code for steps they got right yesterday. With Coral, your agents build and reuse a shared library of proven tool-calling code.

Coral is now used by thousands of developers at more than 450 companies for safer, more efficient agent work in customer support, SecOps, business intelligence, SRE and more.

Quickstart · Download

In this example, an agent posts unreviewed PRs to Slack for the first time. The agent searches for tools and runs a program. It isn't allowed to post to Slack without approval, so the user approves it before it posts. Coral saves the workflow as a function. The next day, the agent runs the same task by calling the saved function.

Get started

  1. Install Coral.

    • For yourself: download the desktop app for macOS, Linux, or Windows from the releases page.
    • For your team: run a shared server with Docker Compose or Kubernetes.

  2. Add a provider. A provider is one service your agents can use, such as GitHub or Linear. Pick one from the catalog, or bring your own OpenAPI document or MCP server. By default, tools that read data run right away and everything else needs your approval. See Add a provider.

  3. Connect your agent. Copy your workspace's MCP URL from the Coral UI and add it to your MCP client:

    claude mcp add --scope user --transport http coral <your-mcp-url>   # Claude Code
codex mcp add coral --url <your-mcp-url>                            # Codex

    For Cursor, VS Code, OpenCode, and other clients, see Connect an MCP client.

  4. Ask a question. Ask your agent something that uses that provider, such as "What are my open pull requests?" Once a task works, Coral saves it as a function your agent can run in one step next time.

Why Coral

MCP tool scopes are often broader than an agent use case requires, and agents waste time and tokens repeatedly figuring out how to do work that's been done before. Coral addresses these problems by saving proven tool-call programs in libraries of reusable functions. Functions improve how your agents access your data and execute work:

  • Precise control. You can limit agents to approved functions only, not everything an MCP tool permits. Security approves "look up an order's refund status," not the whole payments API.
  • Cheaper models, same accuracy. With saved functions, a smaller model performs like a bigger one. For many tasks, this means Opus 5.5 accuracy at Haiku 5.5 cost.
  • Faster, leaner agents. With saved functions, agents finished work 30% faster and at 32% lower token cost on average.
  • Training data you own. Each run leaves a structured trace of the goal, the function used and the outcome that works well for post-training your own model.

From one developer's laptop to an enterprise cloud, Coral fits your stack:

  • Runs on your infrastructure. Coral runs anywhere from a laptop to your own cloud, with zero data egress.
  • Open source. Coral is Apache 2.0. Coral Enterprise adds organization-wide governance and support.
  • Any agent, any system. It works with any AI app or agent that supports MCP. You can connect anything with an MCP server or OpenAPI spec, including more than 5,000 databases and SaaS tools.

How Coral works

Agents write programs. To use tools, an agent writes a short TypeScript program. One program can call several tools, filter the results and return only what the task needs. Less raw data passes through the model's context.

Coral runs them on rails. Each program runs in a sandbox, system credentials never appear in the agent's context or code, and every call is checked against your policy before it reaches the system behind it. Policies can also require a person to approve it.

What works becomes a function. When a program succeeds, Coral saves it as a code function. Your library of proven tool-calling code grows with each task. Agents search that library and reuse, edit and share functions across your team instead of starting over.

Agents never hold credentials. Coral stores your tokens and adds them to each call. Programs run in an isolated sandbox with no secrets, no network access, and no imports, and every run is attributed to the person or agent that started it.

graph LR
    Agent["Your agent"] -->|"exec: run a program"| MCP["Coral MCP server"]
    You["You"] -->|"providers, policy, approvals"| UI["Coral UI"]

    subgraph Coral["Coral (your laptop or server)"]
        MCP --> Run["Program runs in a sandbox"]
        Run <--> FN["Saved functions"]
        UI --> Gate["Policy check and credentials"]
        Run --> Gate
    end

    Gate --> GH["GitHub"]
    Gate --> SL["Slack"]
    Gate --> Own["Your OpenAPI or MCP service"]

The agent sends Coral programs through the exec tool. A program calls coral.workspace.search to find the tools the agent can use and read their TypeScript signatures. Then the agent sends a program that does the work. This one finds open pull requests that have no reviewer and posts them to Slack:

const { data: pulls } = await coral.providers.github.pulls.list({
    owner: "withcoral",
    repo: "coral",
    state: "open",
});

const unreviewed = pulls.filter((pull) => pull.requested_reviewers.length === 0);

await coral.providers.slack.chat.postMessage({
    channel: "#engineering",
    text: unreviewed.map((pull) => `#${pull.number} ${pull.title}`).join("\n"),
});

return unreviewed.map((pull) => pull.number);

Coral adds the credentials and checks each call against your policy. If posting to Slack needs approval, the run pauses there until you approve it. Only the pull request numbers go back to the agent, not the full GitHub response. The run happens on the Coral server, not in your agent, so it carries on even if the agent disconnects.

Once this works, Coral saves the program as a function. Next time, the agent calls it in one step as coral.functions.<name>(), instead of finding the tools and writing the program again.

To learn about providers, accounts, policy, and workspaces, read Concepts.

For teams and enterprise

Coral is open source under the Apache License 2.0. Running it for a team? See Run a shared server.

Coral Enterprise adds organization-wide governance and support, including SSO, advanced access controls, an immutable audit log, and support SLAs. See Enterprise or book a demo.

Development

To run Coral from a checkout, follow the development guide.

Community

Ask questions, share ideas, and show what you built in our Discord or on GitHub issues.

Security

Do not report security issues in public issues or pull requests. See SECURITY.md.

Coral is ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certified. Provider API calls run in an isolated sandbox, approvals are logged, and the Enterprise plan adds SAML and SCIM provisioning, advanced RBAC and an immutable audit log.

License

Coral is licensed under the Apache License 2.0. See LICENSE.

The ee/ directory holds Enterprise Edition code under its own licence, ee/LICENSE. A plain cargo build at the repository root builds only Apache-2.0 code. NOTICE sets out which licence covers which files.

Upgrade from Coral 0.x

Coral v1 replaces the SQL interface with TypeScript programs. It starts from fresh state and does not convert what 0.x stored. If Coral finds 0.x state, it tells you at startup. See Upgrade from Coral 0.x.
